  • Puzzle 2: How Kotlin calls Apple

    Kotlin/Native ships platform libraries: prebuilt Kotlin bindings for each target's native libraries. On Apple targets they cover Apple's frameworks, such as Foundation and UIKit, so code in iosMain can import platform.UIKit.UIDevice and call it like Kotlin. They exist only on Apple targets, which is why such calls live in iosMain, never in commonMain.

The problem

From the next puzzle on, Swift code calls your Kotlin. You've never read Swift, iOS's language, never opened Xcode, Apple's IDE, and you don't know what an iOS screen is made of. What's the smallest picture you need?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

Four names, each with its Android twin:

iOSWhat it isOn Android
SwiftThe language of iOS appsKotlin
XcodeApple's IDE, which builds and runs the appAndroid Studio
UIKitApple's framework for screens: buttons, lists, textthe View system
view controllerManages one screen's UI elements and reacts to the useran Activity or Fragment

A minimal screen in Swift:

import UIKit

class GreetingViewController: UIViewController {
    let label = UILabel()           // let is Kotlin's val

    override func viewDidLoad() {   // like onCreate
        super.viewDidLoad()
        label.text = "Hello"
        label.frame = view.bounds
        label.autoresizingMask = [.flexibleWidth, .flexibleHeight]
        view.addSubview(label)
    }
}

Swift will feel close to Kotlin: classes, override, optional types written with ?, and lambdas (Swift has its own name for them, coming in puzzle 8). Newer iOS apps often use SwiftUI, Apple's declarative UI, the way newer Android apps use Compose; KMP works with both.

Where does your Kotlin fit? It becomes a library this app imports (puzzle 5), and Swift code, often inside a view controller, calls it.

The analogy

Moving to a city where the streets have different names but the same layout. "Main Street" is "Hauptstraße"; once you have the map of names, you find your way.

Which iOS piece plays the role of an Activity?

Sources
  • Apple: UIViewController ("A view controller's main responsibilities include the following: Updating the contents of the views, usually in response to changes to the underlying data; Responding to user interactions with views")
  • The Swift Programming Language: The Basics (constants are declared with let, variables with var)

What you now know

iOS apps are written in Swift, in Xcode, Apple's IDE. Screens are built with UIKit, Apple's screen framework (or the newer SwiftUI). A view controller manages one screen's UI elements and reacts to the user, much like an Activity or Fragment. Swift looks like Kotlin: let is val, var is var, and a class can subclass UIViewController the way yours subclasses Activity.
